{{Short description|Theorem in temporal logic}}
In [[mathematical logic]] and [[computer science]], '''Gabbay's separation theorem''' states that any formula in [[linear temporal logic]] (LTL) with past operators can be rewritten as a boolean combination of formulas that are only concerned with the past, present, or future.<ref>{{citation|title=Handbook of Temporal Reasoning in Artificial Intelligence|volume=1|series=Foundations of Artificial Intelligence|first1=Michael David|last1=Fisher|first2=Dov M.|last2=Gabbay|first3=Lluis|last3=Vila|publisher=Elsevier|year=2005|isbn=9780080533360|page=150|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ajsvo6jWNhgC&pg=PA150}}.</ref> This theorem was stated<ref>{{Citation |last=Gabbay |first=Dov M. |chapter=Expressive Functional Completeness in Tense Logic (Preliminary report) |date=1981 |title=Aspects of Philosophical Logic: Some Logical Forays into Central Notions of Linguistics and Philosophy |pages=91–117 |editor-last=Mönnich |editor-first=Uwe |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-8384-7_4 |access-date= |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-8384-7_4 |isbn=978-94-009-8384-7}}</ref> and proven by [[Dov Gabbay]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gabbay |first=Dov |date=1989 |editor-last=Banieqbal |editor-first=B. |editor2-last=Barringer |editor2-first=H. |editor3-last=Pnueli |editor3-first=A. |chapter=The declarative past and imperative future |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-51803-7_36 |title=Temporal Logic in Specification |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=398 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=409–448 |doi=10.1007/3-540-51803-7_36 |isbn=978-3-540-46811-0|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Expressive Completeness ===
A formula is separated if it is a boolean combination of formulas that are only concerned with the past, present, or future. An arbitrary [[temporal logic]] has the separation property if each formula is equivalent to a separated formula. Gabbay shows that a temporal logic that can express the future operator <math>\mathbf F</math> and the past operator <math>\mathbf P</math> of LTL has the separation property if and only if the logic is [[Completeness (logic)|expressively complete]]. Here, a logic is expressively complete if it is expressively equivalent to the [[Monadic predicate calculus|monadic first-order logic of order]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Hodkinson |first1=Ian |last2=Reynolds |first2=Mark |date=2005 |title=Separation - Past, Present, and Future |url=https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~imh/papers/sep.pdf |journal=We Will Show Them! |issue=2 |pages=117–142}}</ref> Separation was first used to prove [[Kamp's theorem]]. Before, the only known method to prove expressive completeness was a pure syntactic argument.

An example of a logic without the separation property is LTL restricted to the operators <math>\mathbf F</math> and <math>\mathbf P</math>. The formula <math>\mathbf F (a \land \neg \mathbf P \neg b)</math> cannot be separated, where <math>a, b</math> are atomic propositions.<ref name=":0" /> LTL restricted to the next operator <math>\mathbf X</math> and the yesterday operator <math>\mathbf Y</math> has the separation property, but is not expressively complete as it cannot express <math>\mathbf F</math>.

=== Expressiveness of Past Operators ===
Gabbay showed that LTL formulas can be separated. When evaluating a formula over the natural numbers at time 0, formulas only concerning the past are trivial as there is no past at time 0. Thus, every LTL formula using past operators has an equivalent form without past operators at time 0. That is, the addition of past operators do not increase the expressive power of LTL.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov |last2=Pnueli |first2=Amir |last3=Shelah |first3=Saharon |last4=Stavi |first4=Jonathan |title=Proceedings of the 7th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT symposium on Principles of programming languages - POPL '80 |chapter=On the temporal analysis of fairness |date=1980-01-28   |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/567446.567462  |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=163–173 |doi=10.1145/567446.567462 |isbn=978-0-89791-011-8|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> A corollary is that [[CTL*]] with past operators has the same expressive power as CTL* over rooted trees.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kupferman |first1=Orna |last2=Pnueli |first2=Amir |last3=Vardi |first3=Moshe Y. |date=2012 |title=Once and for all |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022000011000857 |journal=[[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]] |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=981–996 |doi=10.1016/j.jcss.2011.08.006 |via=Elsevier Science Direct}}</ref> Hodkinson and Reynolds suggest that this is the reason researchers tend to use future-only versions of LTL, [[Computation tree logic|CTL]], and CTL*.<ref name=":0" /> While LTL with past and LTL have the same expressive power, the inclusion of past operators can make formulas exponentially more succinct.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Markey |first=Nicolas |date=2003 |title=Temporal Logic with Past is Exponentially More Succinct |url=https://hal.science/hal-01194627 |journal=Bulletin- European Association for Theoretical Computer Science |volume=79 |pages=122–128}}</ref>

=== Normal Forms ===
The separation theorem is used to prove various [[Canonical form|normal forms]] for temporal formulas.<ref name=":0" />

==== Safety-Liveness Form ====
Lichtenstein et al. gives us the ''safety-liveness form'',<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lichtenstein |first1=Orna |last2=Pnueli |first2=Amir |last3=Zuck |first3=Lenore |date=1985 |editor-last=Parikh |editor-first=Rohit |chapter=The glory of the past |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-15648-8_16 |title=Logics of Programs |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=193 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=196–218 |doi=10.1007/3-540-15648-8_16 |isbn=978-3-540-39527-0|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> where every formula in LTL is equivalent to a formula of the following form, where <math>a_i, b_i</math> are boolean combinations of atomic propositions:

<math>\bigvee_{i = 1}^n (\mathbf G \mathbf F a_i) \land (\mathbf F \mathbf G b_i)</math>

==== Separated Normal Form ====
Fisher gives us the ''separated normal form'',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fisher |first=Michael |date=1997 |title=A Normal Form for Temporal Logics and its Applications in Theorem-Proving and Execution |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8133496 |journal=Journal of Logic and Computation |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=429–456 |doi=10.1093/logcom/7.4.429 |issn=1465-363X}}</ref> where each formula in LTL can be written in the following form, such that each <math>P_i</math> is only concerned with the past, and <math>F_i</math> is only concerned with the future:

<math>\mathbf G\left(\bigwedge_{i = 1}^n P_i \to F_i \right)</math>

This form has been used for specifications in executable temporal logic, where <math>F_i</math> can be executed when the current history satisfies <math>P_i</math>. [[Concurrent MetateM|MetateM]] is an example of a language that uses this paradigm.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barringer |first1=H. |last2=Fisher |first2=M. |last3=Gabbay |first3=D. |last4=Gough |first4=G. |last5=Owens |first5=R. |date=1995-09-01 |title=MetateM: An introduction |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01211631 |journal=Formal Aspects of Computing |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=533–549 |doi=10.1007/BF01211631 |issn=1433-299X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
